title: Heaps, heapify, buildHeap, heap sort, priority queues
summary: Say why a priority queue needs a heap; read a heap as a tree and as an array with the index formulas; trace heapify, buildHeap and heapSort; explain why buildHeap is O(n) and heap sort is O(n log n) with O(1) space; and run insert and extract on a priority queue.
sourceNote: Lecture 8 'Heaps, Heap Sort, Priority Queues' (Sep 16) slides, HW 8, CLRS ch. 6. Real-world notes are general industry practice.

sections.heading: The big picture: always hand over the most urgent thing

blocks.md: Stacks hand you the newest item, queues the oldest. Lots of real problems want neither: they want the **most important** item, while new items keep arriving. That's a **priority queue**, and a **heap** is the clever structure that makes it fast. Along the way you get a third n log n sort that needs no extra memory.

data.note: Patients keep arriving, so re-sorting everyone each time would be too slow. A heap keeps just enough order to find the max fast.

blocks.caption: Poon's emergency room: arrival order vs urgency order.

blocks.body: A container where each item has a priority. Operations: **insert(x)**, **extract()** (remove and return the highest priority), **peek()**, **isEmpty()**.

blocks.md: **Why not just keep a sorted list?** Inserting into a sorted array costs O(n) shifts. Keeping it unsorted makes extract cost O(n) to find the max. A heap makes **both** O(log n) by keeping only a partial order: just enough to know where the max is.
blocks.label: why

blocks.body: A **complete** binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills left to right) where **every parent ≥ its children**. Consequence: the maximum is always at the root. A **min-heap** flips the inequality; the minimum is at the root. Lecture 8 uses max-heaps throughout.

blocks.md: A heap does not say the left child is smaller than the right. It does not say the array is sorted. It does not let you find the second-largest quickly without extracting the first. The only promise is the one line: parent ≥ children, on every edge. Everything else follows from that plus the complete shape.

blocks.caption: The same ten numbers drawn two ways. The tree is how you think; the array is what the computer stores. Read the tree level by level, left to right, and you get the array.

blocks.body: **Index formulas: 0-based, memorize** Left child of i: **2i + 1**. Right child: **2i + 2**. Parent: **⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋**. First leaf: **⌊n / 2⌋** (every index from there on has no children). He uses 0-based indexing; CLRS uses 1-based (2i, 2i+1, ⌊i/2⌋): don't mix them on the exam.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Why there are no pointers** Because the tree is complete, reading it level by level, left to right, gives one unbroken run of nodes with no holes. So position-in-that-reading *is* the array index, and the arithmetic above recovers the shape. No pointers means no extra memory per node and no chasing references around memory: the heap is one contiguous block.
blocks.slide: Why a complete tree fits in an array

blocks.md: **When you see an index, draw the family.** For index i, say out loud: 'my kids are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, my parent is (i − 1) / 2 rounded down.' For i = 3: kids 7 and 8, parent 1. Two seconds, and every heap question gets easier.

blocks.title: Your turn: the index formulas
blocks.task: Write `left(i)`, `right(i)` and `parent(i)` (0-based), then `is_max_heap(a)`: True when every item is ≤ its parent.
blocks.check:
assert (left(0), right(0)) == (1, 2), "The root's children are at 1 and 2."
assert (left(3), right(3)) == (7, 8), "Index 3's children: 2·3 + 1 = 7 and 2·3 + 2 = 8."
assert parent(7) == 3 and parent(8) == 3, "7 and 8 are both children of 3: (7 − 1) // 2 = 3 and (8 − 1) // 2 = 3."
assert parent(1) == 0 and parent(2) == 0, "1 and 2 are the root's children."
assert is_max_heap([16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]) is True, "[16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1] is a max-heap."
assert is_max_heap([16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]) is False, "In [16, 4, 10, 14, …], index 1 (4) has a child 14 that's bigger: not a heap."
assert is_max_heap([]) is True and is_max_heap([5]) is True, "Empty and one-item arrays are heaps."
hints: left = 2i + 1, right = 2i + 2.
parent = (i − 1) // 2 (integer division rounds down).
is_max_heap: `all(a[parent(i)] >= a[i] for i in range(1, len(a)))`.
blocks.success: Those three one-line formulas are the whole reason a heap needs no pointers.

blocks.prompt: In an array of 12 elements, what are the children of index 4, the parent of index 11, and which indexes are leaves?
blocks.answer: Children of 4: 9 and 10. Parent of 11: ⌊10/2⌋ = 5. Leaves: ⌊12/2⌋ = 6 onward, i.e. indexes 6–11.

blocks.body: Fix **one** node: if a[i] is smaller than a child, swap it with its **larger** child and repeat from there, until it's bigger than both children or reaches a leaf. It assumes both subtrees under i are already heaps.

blocks.title: heapify(a, 1): the 4 sinks to where it belongs (Lecture 8)

frames.caption: heapify(a, 1): a[1] = 4 is smaller than a child, but both subtrees below it are already heaps. Let it sink.
heapify(1): 4 vs its children (14, 7). The largest is 14 at index 3, and it's bigger than 4.
Swap: 14 moves up, 4 sinks to index 3. Keep going from there.
heapify(3): 4 vs its children (2, 8). The largest is 8 at index 8, and it's bigger than 4.
Swap: 8 moves up, 4 sinks to index 8. Keep going from there.
4 reached a leaf (index 8 has no children). Stop.

blocks.md: **Always swap with the LARGER child.** If you swapped with the smaller one, the bigger child would end up under a smaller parent and you'd break the heap you were fixing. Bigger child goes up; the sinking value goes down.
blocks.label: think

blocks.title: `n` is the heap size: which may be smaller than a.length during heapSort. The recursion follows the sinking element down.

blocks.md: heapify assumes the two subtrees *below* i are already valid heaps; it only fixes i itself. Each call does a constant amount of work and moves one level down, so it makes at most (height of the tree) calls. A complete tree with n nodes has height ⌊log₂ n⌋ (Chapter 0: halving). **heapify is O(log n).**

**Slide 21, 'Common misconception'** heapify does NOT sort the array, and it does NOT build a heap from scratch. It repairs a *single* out-of-place value at node i, trusting that everything below is already a heap. Poon put this on its own slide; expect a true/false or short answer on it.

blocks.title: Your turn: write heapify
blocks.task: Write `heapify(a, i, n)` for a max-heap of size n (the part a[0..n−1]). Loop: find the largest of a[i] and its children that exist (index < n); if that's i, stop; otherwise swap and continue from the child.
blocks.starter:
def heapify(a, i, n):
    while True:
        l, r = 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        largest = i
        # if l < n and a[l] > a[largest]: largest = l   (same for r)
        # if largest == i: stop; else swap a[i], a[largest] and set i = largest
        return

a = [16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]
heapify(a, 1, len(a))
print(a)    # expect [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]
blocks.check:
a = [16, 4, 10, 14, 7, 9, 3, 2, 8, 1]
heapify(a, 1, len(a))
assert a == [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1], f"heapify(a, 1) on the slide's array should give [16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1]. Got {a}."
b = [1, 5, 9]
heapify(b, 0, 3)
assert b == [9, 5, 1], f"The root must swap with its LARGER child: [1, 5, 9] → [9, 5, 1]. Got {b}."
c = [3, 9, 8, 100]
heapify(c, 0, 3)
assert c == [9, 3, 8, 100], f"Only the first n items are the heap: with n = 3, index 3 (100) must be ignored. Got {c}."
hints: Two ifs pick the largest: compare a[l] and a[r] with a[largest], only when l < n / r < n.
`if largest == i: return`.
Otherwise swap `a[i], a[largest] = a[largest], a[i]` and set `i = largest`.
blocks.success: One path down the tree, at most log n swaps: heapify is O(log n). Everything else in this chapter is built from it.

sections.heading: buildHeap: any array → a heap, in O(n)

blocks.body: Turn any array into a max-heap by calling heapify on every non-leaf, **from the last one (index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1) back to the root**.

frames.caption: buildHeap on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Leaves (index 3 and up) are already tiny heaps. Start at the last non-leaf, index 2, and walk back to the root.
heapify(2): fix the subtree rooted at index 2 (value 3).
3 is smaller than its bigger child 7: swap. 3 sinks to index 6.
heapify(1): fix the subtree rooted at index 1 (value 2).
2 is smaller than its bigger child 5: swap. 2 sinks to index 4.
heapify(0): fix the subtree rooted at index 0 (value 1).
1 is smaller than its bigger child 7: swap. 1 sinks to index 2.
1 is smaller than its bigger child 6: swap. 1 sinks to index 5.
Done: [7, 5, 6, 4, 2, 1, 3] is a max-heap. Every parent ≥ its children, and the max, 7, is at the root.

blocks.md: **Why bottom-up?** heapify(i) only works if both subtrees under i are already heaps. Going from the bottom up guarantees that: by the time you reach a node, everything below it has been fixed. Leaves are one-item heaps, so they need nothing.
blocks.label: why

blocks.title: Start at the last non-leaf and walk toward the root, heapifying each. Going bottom-up is what guarantees heapify's precondition: by the time we reach i, both of its subtrees have already been fixed.

data.summary: ≤ 11 swaps for n = 15: about n, not n log n

blocks.caption: Why buildHeap is O(n). Each box is one node, labeled with how far it can sink at most. Most nodes are near the bottom and can barely move.
buildHeap, bottom-up, on your array: it starts at the last non-leaf and each heapify is shown as the array and as the tree. Try the check's [3, 9, 2, 1, 4, 5] and confirm heapify runs on 2, 1, 0.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The non-obvious runtime** There are about n/2 calls to heapify, each 'O(log n)', so the lazy answer is O(n log n). But most of those calls are cheap. Half the nodes are leaves (cost 0: we skip them). A quarter sit one level up and can sink at most 1 step. An eighth can sink at most 2. Add it up: n/4·1 + n/8·2 + n/16·3 + …: a series whose sum is about n, not n log n. Poon states O(n) on slide 25; the sentence to say is **'most nodes are near the bottom, so most heapify calls are short.'**
blocks.slide: Why O(n), not O(n log n)
blocks.slideNotes: The intuition without the algebra: half of all nodes are **leaves** and cost zero sifts. A quarter sit one level up and sift at most once. Only ONE node: the root: can ever pay the full log n. So the expensive nodes are vanishingly rare, and the total collapses to plain n. Compare to inserting n items one at a time, where EVERY item can pay log n on its way up. This 'most nodes are near the bottom' argument is a favorite short-answer question, and it's the same geometric-series-converges idea as Chapter 0's ##sum of halves → 2n## trick.

blocks.prompt: buildHeap on [3, 9, 2, 1, 4, 5]. Which indexes get heapified, in what order, and what's the result?
blocks.answer: n = 6, so i = 2, 1, 0. heapify(2): 2 vs child 5 → [3,9,5,1,4,2]. heapify(1): 9 vs 1, 4 → fine. heapify(0): 3 vs 9, 5 → swap with 9 → [9,3,5,1,4,2]; then 3 vs 1, 4 → swap with 4 → [9,4,5,1,3,2].

sections.heading: heapSort: pull the max out, n times

blocks.body: buildHeap once. Then repeat: swap the root (the max) with the last item of the heap, shrink the heap by one, heapify the root.

blocks.caption: heapSort: swap the max to the end, shrink the heap, heapify the root, repeat. The settled tail turns green; the tree shows only what is still in the heap.

rows: O(n) build + n × O(log n) heapify = **O(n log n)**: always, no bad input
**O(1)**: everything happens inside the input array
**No**: the swaps can reorder equal elements
Memory-limited or embedded systems: guaranteed O(n log n) with no extra array

blocks.md: **Use heap sort** when you need a guaranteed n log n **and** can't afford extra memory: embedded devices, kernels, systems with a hard memory budget. **Prefer merge sort** when you need stability (equal items keep their order). **Prefer quicksort** (next chapter) when average speed matters most. Real libraries often use heap sort as a safety net inside quicksort (introsort).
blocks.label: when

blocks.body: Calling heap sort stable. It isn't: the swap of the root to the end can jump an item over equal items.

blocks.prompt: Why is merge sort O(n) space while heap sort is O(1)?
blocks.answer: Merge needs a temporary array so it doesn't overwrite unread elements while merging. Heap sort only ever swaps two positions inside the input array.

sections.heading: Priority queue: insert and extract, O(log n) each

blocks.md: Lectures 2–3: an ADT is the contract, the implementation is the machinery. **Priority queue** is the contract: insert(x with a priority), extract the highest priority, peek, isEmpty. **Heap** is the machinery that makes each of those O(log n) or better. On an exam, 'priority queue' is the answer to *which ADT*, 'heap' is the answer to *how*.

frames.caption: insert(9): put it at the end, index 5, so the tree stays complete. But 9 may be bigger than its parent.
Parent 7 (index 2 = ⌊(5 − 1) / 2⌋) is smaller than 9.
Swap: 9 trickles up to index 2.
Parent 8 (index 0 = ⌊(2 − 1) / 2⌋) is smaller than 9.
Swap: 9 trickles up to index 0.
9 reached the root: it's the new maximum. At most log n swaps.
extract() on [9, 8, 7, 5, 3, 2]: the answer is the root, 9.
Move the LAST item (2) to the root so the tree stays complete, and take 9 out.
heapify(0): 2 vs its children (8, 7). The largest is 8 at index 1, and it's bigger than 2.
Swap: 8 moves up, 2 sinks to index 1. Keep going from there.
heapify(1): 2 vs its children (5, 3). The largest is 5 at index 3, and it's bigger than 2.
Swap: 5 moves up, 2 sinks to index 3. Keep going from there.
2 reached a leaf (index 3 has no children). Stop.
extract() returned 9. The heap [8, 5, 7, 2, 3] is valid again after at most log n swaps.

blocks.caption: Now you drive: insert a big number and watch it climb, then extractMax and watch the replacement sink. The counter compares the swaps with the tree's height.

blocks.body: append at the end (keeps the tree complete), then swap upward with the parent while parent < x. **O(log n)**: one path up.
save a[0]; move the last element to a[0]; shrink; heapify(0). **O(log n)**: one path down.
from a batch of n items: **O(n)**: cheaper than n inserts (n log n).
'future lecture': it's what Dijkstra's algorithm needs.

blocks.md: **Priority queues quietly run a lot of software.** Your operating system picks the next program to run from a priority queue. Game engines and web servers keep a queue of timed events ordered by 'when'. Google Maps-style shortest routes use Dijkstra's algorithm, which is a priority queue of 'closest unvisited place'. Python ships one as `heapq`; Java as `PriorityQueue`.
blocks.label: world

blocks.title: See it: an ER with Python's heapq
blocks.task: Python's `heapq` is a **min**-heap on a plain list. To pop the most urgent first, push `(-urgency, name)`. Run it, then add a patient with urgency 10 midway.
blocks.starter:
import heapq

er = []
for name, urgency in [("A", 2), ("B", 9), ("C", 4)]:
    heapq.heappush(er, (-urgency, name))      # negate: min-heap acts as max-heap
    print("arrived:", name, "urgency", urgency, "| next up:", er[0][1])

heapq.heappush(er, (-7, "D"))
print("D arrives (7). Treating in order:")
while er:
    neg, name = heapq.heappop(er)
    print("  treat", name, "urgency", -neg)

blocks.title: Picking the structure from a story
blocks.body:
Tasks with priorities arrive continuously; the system must always work on the highest-priority task next. Which structure, which operations, what cost?

1. 'Arrive continuously' → we need cheap insert. 'Highest priority next' → we need cheap take-the-max. That pair is the priority queue ADT.
2. Implement it as a **max-heap**: insert is O(log n), extract-max is O(log n).
3. If a batch of tasks exists at startup, buildHeap them in O(n) instead of inserting one at a time.
blocks.answer: Priority queue via max-heap; insert + extract, both O(log n)
blocks.slideNotes: This homework problem is a miniature of how priority queues run the real world: OS process schedulers pick the highest-priority ready thread from a PQ, Dijkstra's shortest-path (coming in the graphs unit) pops the closest unvisited city from a PQ, and every ER triage board is one. The pattern to recognize: whenever a problem says 'always take the most-X item next' and items keep arriving, the answer is a heap: O(log n) per event instead of re-sorting everything, O(n log n), on every arrival.

blocks.prompt: Max-heap vs min-heap: and give a real use for a min-heap.
blocks.answer: Max-heap: parent ≥ children, root is the max. Min-heap: parent ≤ children, root is the min. Min-heap uses: Dijkstra's shortest path (always take the closest unvisited vertex), event simulation ordered by earliest time, merging k sorted lists.

blocks.md: **Heap in one paragraph.** A complete binary tree in an array (children 2i+1, 2i+2; parent ⌊(i−1)/2⌋) with parent ≥ children. heapify(i) sinks one node, O(log n). buildHeap runs heapify from ⌊n/2⌋−1 down to 0, O(n). heapSort = buildHeap + n rounds of swap-to-end + heapify(0), O(n log n) time, O(1) space, unstable. A heap implements the priority-queue ADT with insert and extract in O(log n).

rows: the ADT: insert, extract the highest priority, peek, isEmpty
a complete binary tree where every parent ≥ its children
every level full except the last, which fills left to right
let a[i] sink by swapping with its larger child: O(log n)
heapify every non-leaf from ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 down to 0: O(n)
buildHeap, then n × (swap root to end, heapify): O(n log n), O(1) space, not stable
insert's move: swap with the parent while bigger

exercises.title: Children of 5
exercises.prompt: In a 0-based heap array, what are the indexes of the children of index 5? Answer like 11, 12.
hints: left = 2i + 1.
right = 2i + 2.
solution: Children: 11, 12.
exercises.why: Index arithmetic replaces pointers; getting it right is the first line of every heap trace.

exercises.title: Parent of 9
exercises.prompt: What is the parent index of index 9?
hints: parent = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋.
exercises.why: Trickle-up in insert uses this formula at every step.

exercises.title: Which child?
exercises.prompt: heapify finds a[i] smaller than both children. Which child does it swap with, and why?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: After the swap, the child you picked becomes the parent.
It must be ≥ the other child.
So pick the larger.
exercises.why: This is the most common heapify mistake on a hand trace.

choices.text: The smaller one, to move less
choices.feedback: Then the bigger child would sit under a smaller parent: broken heap.

choices.text: The larger one, so the new parent is ≥ both children
choices.feedback: Right: the larger child becomes the parent of the other child, so the property holds there.
It matters: the wrong choice breaks the heap one level down.

exercises.title: Where buildHeap starts
exercises.prompt: buildHeap on an array of n = 10. Which index is heapified first?
hints: First leaf = ⌊n/2⌋ = 5.
Start one before the first leaf.
solution: Leaves: 5 to 9.
Last non-leaf: 4.
exercises.why: Starting at the last non-leaf skips half the array: the leaves are already one-item heaps.

exercises.title: buildHeap's cost
exercises.prompt: Why is buildHeap O(n) even though it calls heapify (O(log n)) about n/2 times?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: How far can a node near the bottom sink?
Count nodes per level times their max sink distance.
exercises.why: A classic example of a loose Big-O bound vs a tight one.

choices.text: It isn't; it's O(n log n)
choices.feedback: The loose bound is n log n, but the tight one is n.

choices.text: Most nodes are near the bottom and can only sink a level or two
choices.feedback: Right: half the nodes are leaves (0 work), a quarter sink ≤ 1, an eighth ≤ 2… The sum stays under n.
Each call can still be log n for the nodes near the top.

exercises.title: Heap sort's space
exercises.prompt: How much extra memory does heap sort use, and is it stable?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Does heap sort allocate a second array?
No: it swaps within a.
Can equal items change order? Yes.
exercises.why: In-place + guaranteed n log n is heap sort's selling point for memory-tight systems.

choices.feedback: It's in place, but the long-distance swaps break stability.
Right: everything happens inside the input array, and swapping the root to the end can jump equal items.

exercises.title: insert's cost
exercises.prompt: What does insert(x) cost on a heap of n items, and why?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Where does x go first?
At the end: index n.
Then it swaps upward, at most log n times.
exercises.why: Both PQ operations follow one root-to-leaf path: that's why heaps beat sorted arrays for this job.

choices.feedback: Appending is O(1), but x may be bigger than its parent.

choices.text: O(log n): append, then trickle up at most the tree's height
choices.feedback: Right: one path from a leaf to the root, height log n.

choices.text: O(n): shift items to make room
choices.feedback: Nothing shifts; it swaps along one path.

exercises.title: Extract by hand
exercises.prompt: extract() on the max-heap [9, 8, 7, 5, 3, 2]. What is the array after the operation? Answer like [a, b, c, d, e].
hints: Return 9; move the last item (2) to the root.
2 vs children 8 and 7: swap with 8.
2 (now at index 1) vs children 5 and 3: swap with 5.
exercises.why: Poon's slide 41–42 example: exactly what the midterm will ask you to trace.

exercises.title: Index arithmetic without the picture
exercises.prompt: A max-heap is stored in an array of 15 elements. Without drawing it: (a) what are the children of index 6? (b) the parent of index 13? (c) which indexes are leaves? (d) if a[6] = 40, what can you say about a[13] and a[14]?
hints: Three formulas: left 2i+1, right 2i+2, parent ⌊(i−1)/2⌋. Just apply them. Leaves start at ⌊n/2⌋.

Two frequent slips: using the 1-based CLRS formulas (2i, 2i+1, ⌊i/2⌋) in a 0-based array, and thinking 'leaves are the last row': with n = 15 the last row happens to be full, but in general leaves are everything from ⌊n/2⌋ on.
For (d): the heap property is only between a node and its own children. Which indexes are 6's children? Then the inequality follows.
solution: (a) Children of 6: 2·6+1 = 13 and 2·6+2 = 14.
(c) Leaves: ⌊15/2⌋ = 7 through 14: eight leaves, exactly half of 15 rounded up.
(d) a[13] ≤ 40 and a[14] ≤ 40, because 13 and 14 are 6's children and a parent is ≥ its children. Nothing is implied about a[13] vs a[14].
exercises.why: Heaps are stored this way because array arithmetic is the fastest thing a CPU does: no pointers to follow, everything in one cache-friendly block. Priority queues in operating systems, Dijkstra's algorithm, and every 'top-k' query run on this arithmetic.

exercises.title: buildHeap, then one extract
exercises.prompt: Run buildHeap on [4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 8, 9] showing the array after each heapify call. Then perform extract() and show the array after the swap and after the heapify.
hints: n = 7 → first leaf is index 3, so heapify runs for i = 2, 1, 0 in that order. For each, compare the node with its two children and swap with the larger if the larger beats the node.
The mistake that costs the most is stopping heapify after one swap. If the sunk value still has children, compare again. In heapify(0) here, the value sinks twice.
For extract: take a[0], move the LAST element to a[0], shrink to 6 elements, then heapify(0) on the 6-element heap: ignore the old last slot.
solution: heapify(2): 3 vs children 8, 9 → swap with 9: [4, 10, 9, 5, 1, 8, 3].
heapify(1): 10 vs 5, 1 → already largest, no change.
heapify(0): 4 vs 10, 9 → swap with 10: [10, 4, 9, 5, 1, 8, 3]; 4 now at index 1 vs children 5, 1 → swap with 5: [10, 5, 9, 4, 1, 8, 3]. Heap built.

extract(): return 10. Move last (3) to root, size 6: [3, 5, 9, 4, 1, 8]. heapify(0): 3 vs 5, 9 → swap with 9: [9, 5, 3, 4, 1, 8]; 3 at index 2 vs child 8 (index 5; index 6 is out of range) → swap: [9, 5, 8, 4, 1, 3].
exercises.why: This is the exact loop inside a task scheduler, a bandwidth shaper, or an event simulator: build once, then extract-the-max forever. If you can trace it, you can read the standard library's PriorityQueue source and know what it costs.

exercises.title: Pick the structure and justify the cost
exercises.prompt: A log system receives a million events per hour and must always report the 100 most severe seen so far, updated in real time. Compare: (A) keep a sorted array of all events, (B) keep a min-heap of size 100, (C) keep a max-heap of all events. Which would you choose and what does each cost per event?

choices.feedback: Inserting into a sorted array is O(n): shifting up to a million elements per event. And you're storing everything when you only need 100.

choices.text: (B) a min-heap holding only the top 100
choices.feedback: Right. The root is the *least severe of the top 100*. New event: if it beats the root, replace the root and heapify: O(log 100), constant in practice. Memory: 100 items.
Insert is O(log n): fine: but 'the top 100' would need 100 extracts (then re-inserts) every time you report, and you store every event forever. A max-heap gives you the max, not the top k.

hints: You only ever need 100 things. What's the one comparison that decides whether a new event belongs among them? Which structure makes *that* item O(1) to find?

The counter-intuitive part is using a MIN-heap to track the MAXIMUM 100. People pick the max-heap by reflex. Ask: to decide if a newcomer joins the top 100, do you need the best of the top 100 or the worst of them?
Think of the top-100 as a club with a bouncer. The bouncer only needs to know the *weakest* current member. A min-heap keeps the weakest at the root.
solution: Keep a min-heap of the 100 most severe events seen so far. Its root is the least severe of those 100.
New event e: if severity(e) ≤ root, discard it in O(1). Otherwise replace the root with e and heapify(0): O(log 100) ≈ 7 steps.
Reporting the top 100 is just reading the heap (or sorting 100 items). Memory stays at 100 no matter how many events arrive.
Sorted array: O(n) per insert. Max-heap of everything: O(log n) insert but O(k log n) to report the top k, plus unbounded memory.
exercises.why: 'Top k of a stream' is one of the most common real problems there is: trending topics, most-viewed pages, hottest CPUs in a fleet: and the min-heap-of-size-k trick is the standard answer. It's also a classic interview question precisely because the reflex answer (max-heap) is wrong.
